contexts.evidence: Table V (p. 100), recognition odour thresholds of an untrained panel of 35 (33-34 observers per gas). contexts.evidence: Miller gives no diameters, only the pressures at which flatus is felt and passed (p. 1005). Passing flatus (54 events): sphincter pressure fell 35 mmHg (0-88), rectal pressure rose 8 mmHg (range -10 to 88). In one-third of passages there was no rectal rise at all (p. 1006). In the ambulatory traces (Figs 4-8, zeroed to atmosphere) resting rectal pressure is about 15-30 mmHg and peaks near 40 mmHg on passage (Fig. 8). So typical driving pressures (about 20-40 mmHg absolute; rise median 8) lie below the 40-55 mmHg FLIP pressures at which the mid canal reaches about 8 mm (sorensen2014). The range of rises (up to 88 mmHg) means some passages exceed them, so 'only at balloon pressures above those that drive flatus' holds for typical passages, not all. The settings also differ: ambulatory vs supine FLIP.

contexts.evidence: The 0-15 mmHg range is for flatus SENSATION (144 events: sphincter -30 mmHg (20-50), rectal +7 mmHg (0-15), rectal >= sphincter in 80%). For PASSAGE (54 events) the rectal rise was 8 mmHg (range -10 to 88), with sphincter pressure falling 35 mmHg (0-88) and equalising with rectal pressure. These were not statistically different from sensation. Passage through a relaxed sphincter is supported (Discussion, p. 1006, which also contrasts with Finlay's closed-sphincter finding).
contexts.suggested_fix: Manometry shows flatus passing through a relaxed sphincter at a median rectal pressure rise of 8\,mmHg (range $-10$ to 88; 0--15\,mmHg when flatus was only sensed) \cite{miller1988b,ronholt1999}, but also against a contracted one \cite{kumar1990}.

contexts.evidence: Fig. 2A (p. 259), healthy volunteers (n = 21) at rest: mid anal canal diameter about 5.3-5.5 mm at 20-30 mL distension, about 8.3 mm at 40 mL and about 13 mm at 50 mL. Text (p. 258): the middle canal had the greatest resistance and usually yielded only at 50 mL. Fig. 4 (p. 260), pressure vs diameter stretch ratio: the healthy mid canal reaches a stretch ratio of 1.5 at about 43 mmHg and 1.8 at about 53 mmHg, with about 1.25 at 30 mmHg. So 'about 8 mm only at about 40+ mmHg' is supported. Caveats: Fig. 2 is plotted against volume, not pressure; subjects were supine after an enema; IFI patients distend about twice as much at >= 30 mmHg. contexts.evidence: Table 4 (p. 387), intensity on a 9-point scale, positive vs negative label (n = 80). I-B acid 7.31 vs 7.46 (+2.1%), pine oil 7.22 vs 7.04 (-2.5%), menthol 7.09 vs 7.24 (+2.1%), violet leaf 6.00 vs 6.75 (+12.5%, p < 0.01), patchouli 6.29 vs 6.45 (+2.5%). Odour x Label interaction F(4,380) = 3.70, p < 0.01. Other intensity effects: label order (negative first 7.00 vs positive first 6.76, +3.6%, p < 0.05); men given positive labels rated odours weaker (6.60 vs about 6.97, about -5%). So 0-3% holds for 4 of 5 odours, but the one significant odour effect was about 12%, and the order and gender effects exceed 3%. Labels were spoken by the experimenter at every presentation ('this is ...'), with a sniff of a few seconds and unlimited re-sniffs. Participants were told the labels, so the 'sign for an unwarned listener not established' clause is consistent. A negative label raised intensity for 4 of 5 odours, while pine oil went the other way.
contexts.suggested_fix: \emph{Expectation.} Measured label effects on rated intensity are small for most odours (about 2--3\%) but reach about 12\% for one \cite{herz2001}; all were measured with the label announced, and their sign for an unwarned listener has not been established \cite{herz2001,djordjevic2008,dalton1999}.
